title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
This document documents the data-cleaning pipeline for the WITS GVC trade dataset. It covers:

Loading the raw trade, sector, and country reference tables
Classifying countries into analytical regions
Merging trade data with sector and region metadata
Reshaping the merged data into long format for downstream analysis

Analysis, plotting, and index-construction steps are intentionally left out of this document — the goal here is a clean, well-documented, reusable dataset.

Option A — download by hand

Open the page above in a browser.
Click Download GVC Trade and save gvc_trade.zip into data.raw/gvc_trade/.
Unzip it. WITS distributes the trade data as one CSV per source (e.g. wiodlr, tiva); after unzipping you should see one or more .csv files inside data.raw/gvc_trade/. title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
Classify countries into regions
We build a Region2 grouping on top of the country table:

Europe — all countries in the UN “Europe” region
ASEAN — countries in the UN “South-eastern Asia” sub-region
N.America — USA, CAN, MEX (NAFTA)
Individually tracked countries: JPN, CHN, KOR
Everything else falls into ROW (rest of world)


eurs  = codelist$iso3c[codelist$un.region.name == "Europe" &
                          !is.na(codelist$iso3c)]

asean = codelist$iso3c[codelist$un.regionsub.name == "South-eastern Asia" &
                          !is.na(codelist$iso3c)]

nafta = c("USA", "CAN", "MEX")

idvs  = c("JPN", "CHN", "KOR")

cty[, Region2 := country]
cty[country %in% eurs,  Region2 := "Europe"]
cty[country %in% asean, Region2 := "ASEAN"]
cty[country %in% nafta, Region2 := "N.America"]
cty[!country %in% c(eurs, asean, nafta, idvs), Region2 := "ROW"]


Sanity check: any countries without a region?

cty[is.na(Region2)]

Empty data.table (0 rows and 4 cols): country,country_name,Region,Region2


If this returns rows, those countries were not matched by countrycode’s region lookup and should be assigned manually before proceeding.

Merge in exporter / importer regions
The region classification built above is joined twice — once for the exporter (exp) and once for the importer (imp).

dt2 = merge(dt2, cty[, .(exp = country, exp_reg = Region2)], by = "exp")
dt2 = merge(dt2, cty[, .(imp = country, imp_reg = Region2)], by = "imp")

Both NA counts should be zero after this step — any non-zero count means some exporter/importer codes in dt don’t have a match in cty and were dropped by the merge (or need to be added to the country table).

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example

Reshape to long format
Two sources are combined:

wiodlr for all years
tiva restricted to years after 2000 (its methodology changes before that point)

  dt2[source == "wiodlr" | (source == "tiva" & t > 2000)| 
        (source=="eora" & t %in% c(1990,1997,2007,2015)),
      .(source,imp, exp, imp_reg, exp_reg,
        sect_name, sect_group,
        t, traditional_trade_int, traditional_trade_fin,
        gvcbp, gvcfp, gvcmix)],

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
This is not an R syntax tutorial — it’s a walkthrough of a real cleaning job: turning a messy, human-formatted Excel file into a tidy dataset ready for analysis and plotting.
The general workflow is always the same, whatever the raw data looks like:

Load the raw file, one sheet/section at a time
Inspect it — look at the actual structure before assuming anything
Clean — rename, reshape, and fix inconsistencies
Handle exceptions — real data always has special cases
Combine the cleaned pieces
Sanity-check with a quick plot before trusting the result
Save the cleaned data so the raw file is never touched again

We’ll follow that exact sequence using the Maddison Project Database (a long-run historical GDP dataset), which has two of the messiest but most common problems in real-world data: data spread across a wide, label-heavy format, and inconsistent structure between sheets.

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
0. Download the raw data
Before any cleaning can happen, the raw file has to exist locally. The Maddison Project Database is published on DataverseNL with a DOI: 10.34894/INZBF2. Downloading it through R (rather than clicking a button in a browser) means the script documents exactly where the data came from, and can be re-run from scratch by anyone.

# The dataverse package defaults to Harvard's Dataverse, so it has to be
# pointed at the right server first.
#Sys.setenv("DATAVERSE_SERVER" = "dataverse.nl")

# Look up the dataset by its DOI
#library(dataverse)
#ds <- get_dataset("10.34894/INZBF2")
#ds$files[, c("filename", "contentType")]

# Download the specific file by name (confirmed from the listing above)
#raw <- get_file("mpd2023_web.xlsx", dataset = "10.34894/INZBF2")

dir.create("../data/raw", showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create("../data/temp", showWarnings = FALSE)
writeBin(raw, "../data/raw/mpd2023_web.xlsx")







Tip



ds$files is worth printing and looking at before downloading anything — never guess a filename. This is the same “inspect before you act” habit that shows up again in the cleaning steps below.


This chunk is set to eval: false since the file only needs to be downloaded once. Run it manually the first time, then leave it off for every subsequent render.

library(readxl)
library(data.table)

mdp <- "../data/raw/mpd2023_web.xlsx"







Note



Keep raw files in a data/raw/ folder and cleaned output in data/temp. Never overwrite the raw file — if a cleaning step turns out to be wrong, you want to be able to start over from the original.

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
1. Load the raw data
The Maddison file has multiple sheets. We start with the “Regional data” sheet, which reports GDP per capita and population by world region.

mdp_region <- read_xlsx(mdp,
                         sheet = "Regional data",
                         skip = 1)

New names:

• `East Asia` -> `East Asia...2`
• `Eastern Europe` -> `Eastern Europe...3`
• `Latin America` -> `Latin America...4`
• `Middle East and North Africa` -> `Middle East and North Africa...5`
• `South and South East Asia` -> `South and South East Asia...6`

• `Western Offshoots` -> `Western Offshoots...9`

• `` -> `...11`

• `Eastern Europe` -> `Eastern Europe...13`

• `Middle East and North Africa` -> `Middle East and North Africa...15`
• `South and South East Asia` -> `South and South East Asia...16`

Note skip = 1 — the first row of the sheet is a title/header banner, not column names. You only know this by opening the file and looking at it first. This is a general rule: never write cleaning code before you’ve visually inspected the raw file yourself.

This one str() call tells us the two problems we need to fix:

Column names are junk like ...1, ...10, ...11 — these come from Excel columns that had no header text, or a header that got interpreted as blank
There are duplicate column names (“Sub Saharan Africa” appears twice — once for GDP per capita, once for population), which R silently renamed by appending numbers

Neither of these is visible from the code alone — they only show up once you actually look at the structure of what got loaded.

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
3. Clean: rename ambiguous columns

setnames(mdp_region, "...1", "date")
setnames(mdp_region, "...10", "World GDPpc")
setnames(mdp_region, "Sub Saharan Africa", "Sub Saharan Africa___1")
setnames(mdp_region, "Sub Saharan SSA", "Sub Saharan Africa___20")
mdp_region[, "...11" := NULL]

Each rename here is fixing a specific, identified problem from step 2 — not a guess. The two “Sub Saharan Africa” columns get a ___1 / ___20 suffix as a deliberate marker: it lets us split them back apart programmatically later, rather than fixing each one by hand.
mdp_region[, "...11" := NULL] drops a column that inspection showed was empty/unused — always confirm a column is genuinely unneeded before deleting it, rather than dropping anything that looks odd.

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
section: 4. Clean: reshape from wide to long
text:
4. Clean: reshape from wide to long
The raw sheet has one column per region — wide format, convenient for a human reading a spreadsheet, but awkward for analysis. melt() converts it to long format: one row per date/region/value combination.

dt <- melt(mdp_region, id.vars = "date")

   c("region", "var") := tstrsplit(variable, " ")]
dt[, c("variable", "id") := NULL]

Notice the pattern: apply the general rule, then explicitly patch the known exception — rather than writing one rule complex enough to cover every case at once. This keeps each step readable and debuggable.

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
section: 7. Load and clean a second sheet with different structure
text:
7. Load and clean a second sheet with different structure
Japan isn’t broken out separately in the regional sheet, so we pull it from the “Full data” sheet (which has one row per country-year) instead:

mdp_jpn <- read_xlsx(mdp, sheet = "Full data")
setDT(mdp_jpn)
str(mdp_jpn)

Classes 'data.table' and 'data.frame':  131144 obs. of  6 variables:
 $ countrycode: chr  "AFG" "AFG" "AFG" "AFG" ...
 $ country    : chr  "Afghanistan" "Afghanistan" "Afghanistan" "Afghanistan" ...
 $ region     : chr  "South and South East Asia" "South and South East Asia" "South and South East Asia" "South and South East Asia" ...
 $ year       : num  1 730 1000 1090 1150 ...
 $ gdppc      : num  NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA ...
 $ pop        : num  NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA ...
 - attr(*, ".internal.selfref")=<externalptr> 



setnames(mdp_jpn,
         c("year", "gdppc", "pop", "country"),
         c("date", "GDPpc", "Population", "region"),
         skip_absent = TRUE)

Renaming to match the column names already used in dt (date, region) is deliberate — it’s what makes the two cleaned pieces combinable in step 8. skip_absent = TRUE means the rename won’t error if a name doesn’t exist, which is a safe default when you’re not 100% sure of every column name in a sheet you didn’t design.

dt2 <- melt(mdp_jpn[countrycode == "JPN"],
            id.vars = c("date", "region"),
            measure.vars = c("GDPpc", "Population"),
            drop = TRUE)

Same wide-to-long reshape as step 4, applied to this differently-shaped source, filtered down to just the one country we need.

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
8. Combine the cleaned pieces

# Real GDP per capita in 2011$
dt3 <- rbindlist(list(dt, dt2), use.names = TRUE, fill = TRUE)

use.names = TRUE matches columns by name rather than position (safer whenever two tables were cleaned separately). fill = TRUE allows columns that exist in one piece but not the other — necessary here since dt and dt2 don’t have identical column sets.
The comment above this line matters as much as the code: always leave a note about units/definitions right next to the data, since it won’t be obvious from the column names alone months later.

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
section: 9. Sanity-check with a plot before saving
text:
9. Sanity-check with a plot before saving

ggpubr::ggline(dt3[variable == "GDPpc" & date > 1900],
               x = "date", y = "value", color = "region",
               numeric.x.axis = TRUE)

Warning: Removed 3 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_line()`).


Warning: Removed 7 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).









This plot isn’t the final deliverable — it’s a cleaning validation step. If a region’s line looks discontinuous, jumps to an implausible value, or is missing entirely, that’s a sign of a cleaning bug, and it’s far easier to catch here than after the data has already been saved and used elsewhere.






Tip



Keep a commented-out line like this for a second variable you’re not currently checking — it costs nothing and makes it trivial to re-check later:
# ggpubr::ggline(dt3[variable=="Population"&date>1900],
#                x="date",y="value",color="region",
#                numeric.x.axis = T)

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
10. Save the cleaned data

fwrite(dt3[!is.na(value)], "../data/temp/madison.csv")

Two decisions worth calling out:

dt3[!is.na(value)] drops rows with no value at the save step, not earlier — keeping NA rows around during cleaning makes it easier to spot where gaps came from, but there’s no reason to ship them in the final file
Saving to .csv in a data/ (not data.raw/) folder means anything downstream (a graphing script, another student, future-you) never needs to re-open the original Excel file or re-run this cleaning again

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
11. Build a companion lookup table
Not every useful output has to be the main dataset. Here we also save a small reference table mapping country codes to regions, which other scripts can join against later:

mdp <- read_xlsx(mdp, sheet = "Full data")
setDT(mdp)
regions <- unique(mdp[, .(countrycode, country, region)])
regions[, .N, by = region]

                         region     N
                         <char> <int>
1:    South and South East Asia    16
2:           Sub Saharan Africa    46
3:               Eastern Europe    32
4: Middle East and North Africa    20
5:                Latin America    26
6:            Western Offshoots     4
7:               Western Europe    19
8:                    East Asia     6

regions[grepl("Western Offshoots", region), .N, by = country]

         country     N
          <char> <int>
1:     Australia     1
2:        Canada     1
3:   New Zealand     1
4: United States     1

fwrite(regions, "../data/temp/madison_regions.csv")

The two .N checks here are, again, checkpoints — confirming the region grouping looks sensible (right number of regions, right countries inside a given region) before trusting the lookup table enough to save it.

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
Summary: the general pattern








Step
What
Why




Load
read_xlsx() one sheet at a time
Different sheets often have different structure


Inspect
str()
Reveals problems (bad names, duplicates) invisible in code alone


Rename
setnames()
Fix ambiguous/duplicate names before reshaping


Reshape
melt()
Wide (human-readable) → long (analysis-ready)


Recover structure
tstrsplit() on encoded names
Turn a naming trick back into real columns


Handle exceptions
Targeted dt[condition, ...] fix
Apply general rule, then patch known special cases


Combine
rbindlist(..., fill = TRUE)
Merge cleaned pieces from different sources


Validate
Quick plot or .N by group
Catch cleaning bugs before they reach saved data


Save
fwrite() to a separate data/ folder
Never re-touch the raw file; downstream work reads the clean version



This same sequence applies to almost any messy raw dataset — the details of what’s messy change, but the order of operations doesn’t.

Began providing technical experts, training, and equipment to Asian countries

Since 1970s:

Gradually aligned with DAC norms (grant element, untying, evaluation)
Adopted global themes (environment, gender, participation)

Japan ODA charter (1992) list philosophies of Japan’s ODA

humanitarian considerations
recognition of interdependence among nations of the international community
environmental consideration
support for self-help efforts of recipient countries





The plan was established in 1950 by Commonwealth nations to promote technical cooperation among the member countries of the British Commonwealth of Nations, with the focus on economic development in South and Southeast Asia.

title: Official Development Assistance

Japan’s Approach vs. DAC Model









Aspect
Japan’s ODA Approach
Typical DAC / Western Approach




Development Philosophy
“Ingredients approach” – emphasizes tangible inputs (infrastructure, technology, industry)
“Framework approach” – focuses on institutions, policy reform, governance


Economic Role of the State
Active state-led industrialization and strategic planning
Market-driven liberalization, minimal state intervention


Aid Objectives
Promote productive capacity, trade, and growth in Asia
Prioritize poverty reduction, welfare, and governance reforms


Aid Modality
Loans and technical cooperation, often tied to Japanese firms
Predominantly grants, focused on social sectors


Underlying Logic
Development as self-help and partnership — supporting recipient ownership through economic buildup
Development as policy reform and conditionality — supporting institutional change

Debates on ODA effectiveness


In theory, ODA effect can be

Positive: use ODA to invest and grow
Non-positive: use ODA to consume luxury goods

Empirical studies:

Aid has no effect on growth (early 1970 studies)
Aid has a positive relationship with growth on average with diminishing returns (1990s studies)
Aid has a conditional relationship with growth:

Good policies (Burnside and Dollar, 2000)
Climate, institutional quality, political conflict, and geography (Hansen and Tarp, 2001)


Each type of aid has different impact on growth:

Humanitarian aid: no direct impact
Infrastructure aid: positive impact (Easterly, 2003)

title: Measurement of Global Value Chains
text:
Trade in Tasks

Traditional trade theory: countries exchange complete, finished goods
Grossman & Rossi-Hansberg (2008): production is unbundled into discrete tasks — design, component sourcing, fabrication, assembly, testing, marketing
Comparative advantage now applies task-by-task, not product-by-product
A task is offshored when it can be performed abroad more cheaply, net of coordination and trade costs



WTO and JETRO-IDE (2011) reframe East Asian trade as evolving “from trade in goods to trade in tasks”
Explains the rise of intra-industry, intra-firm trade in intermediate goods
A country’s export mix reflects which tasks it specializes in, not which whole product it exports

title: Measurement of Global Value Chains
text:
Trade in Value Added

Gross trade statistics double-count intermediate inputs that cross borders multiple times before reaching the final consumer
The Trade in Value Added (TiVA) approach reallocates exports to the country that actually created the value:

Domestic Value Added (DVA): value added by the exporting country itself
Foreign Value Added (FVA): value added by other countries, embodied in imported inputs




Gross exports overstate bilateral imbalances (e.g., the US–China trade deficit narrows substantially once measured in value-added terms)
Value-added trade better reflects which country actually benefits from a given trade flow

title: Measurement of Global Value Chains
text:
Measuring GVC Participation
Backward linkage (backward participation)
\[ \text{Backward} = \frac{FVA}{\text{Gross Exports}} \times 100 \] Forward linkage (forward participation)
\[ \text{Forward} = \frac{DVX}{\text{Gross Exports}} \times 100 \] Total GVC participation = Backward + Forward


Based on the gross export decomposition in Koopman, Wang & Wei (2014), built from international input–output tables
Small, open economies (e.g., ASEAN members) tend to show higher backward participation. They import more of what they need to export
Countries positioned at the start of chains (raw materials, core components, R&D) tend to show higher forward participation
Rule of thumb: Backward ↑ when a country imports a lot of intermediates; Forward ↑ when a country’s intermediates are re-exported by others

title: Measurement of Global Value Chains

GVC intensity and GVC position

How strongly is a country or industry involved in GVC production?

\[
\text{GVC Participation}
=
\text{Pure Backward}
+
\text{Pure Forward}
+
\text{Mixed}
\]

Where does the country or industry tend to operate in the value chain?

\[
Forwardness = \frac{\text{Pure Forward} - \text{Pure Backward}}{\text{Total GVC Participation}}
\]

Summed over all countries, sectors and partners, pure forward activity equals pure backward activity.
At the country-sector level, 0 means pure forward and pure backward are balanced, so the sector is neither mainly at the start nor mainly at the end of chains, relative to the world average. Positive values mean more upstream (supplying inputs), negative values mean more downstream (assembling from imported inputs).
Alternative measures of GVC position include upstreamness (distance of output from final demand) and downstreamness (distance from primary inputs/value added). These measures are conceptually related to, but distinct from, WITS forwardness.

Upstream (high value): design, R&D, core components, precise machinery
Midstream: capital goods exports, management of production networks
Downstream: limited (assembly shifted to China/ASEAN), but could be different for chemicals (pharmaceutical synthesis)

title: Comparative Advantage: The case of Japan
text:
Absolute vs. Comparative advantage

Being better at producing everything is absolute advantage: does not determine what gets traded.
Comparative advantage is about relative opportunity cost: what you give up to produce more unit of something.
Even a country with no absolute advantage in anything still has a comparative advantage in something.

title: Comparative Advantage: The case of Japan
text:
Productivity differences

Core idea: countries export the good where their opportunity cost is lowest.
Japan’s technology edge in precision manufacturing lowers the opportunity cost of producing autos and electronics relative to its trading partners.
In agriculture, Japan has higher opportunity costs, which driving the import patterns

title: Comparative Advantage: The case of Japan
text:
Short-run immobility

Core idea: some factors (land, sector-specific capital) can’t quickly move between industries.
Japan’s farmland and farmers can’t retrain into auto manufacturing overnight.
Despite comparative disadvantage in agriculture, Japan has long-standing protection policy.

title: Comparative Advantage: The case of Japan
text:
Factor abundance

Core idea: countries export goods that intensively use their abundance factor.
Japan is capital- and technology-abundant relative to land and labor.
Japan export capital-intensive goods (car, electronics) and imports land/labor-intensive goods (food, raw materials)

Limits of RCA as a measure

RCA reflects actual trade flows, which are already shaped by tariffs, subsidies, and protection, not a “pure” underlying advantage.
Global value chains: a “Japanese” car may contain parts made in many countries, blurring what RCA is really measuring.
Categorization-sensitive: results can shift depending on how narrowly or broadly a “sector” is defined.

Japan tariff

Source: WTO Tariff Profile (2025)
Tariff line: the most detailed product category in a country’s tariff schedule, identified by a national code (usually 8 to 10 digits, built on the 6-digit HS code). Each tariff line has its own duty rate. “AVG”, “Duty-free in %”, “Max” and “Binding in %” are all calculated over tariff lines, not over trade value.

Final bound duties: the maximum tariff rates Japan has committed to the WTO for each product line. Japan cannot legally raise tariffs above these ceilings.
MFN applied duties: the rates Japan actually charges other WTO members under the Most-Favoured-Nation principle, i.e. the non-discriminatory “normal” tariff, excluding preferential rates under FTAs. Applied rates are at or below bound rates.
AVG: simple average of the ad valorem tariff rates (%) across all lines in the group.
Duty-free in %: share of tariff lines with a zero rate.
Max: the highest single tariff rate in the group (italics mark non-ad valorem rates converted to ad valorem equivalents).
Binding in %: share of tariff lines that are bound at the WTO (100 means every line is bound).
Imports (Share in %): the group’s share of Japan’s total imports.
Imports (Duty-free in %): share of the group’s import value that enters duty-free.

FDI: cross-border investment with a lasting interest and control (commonly a 10% voting-share threshold)

title: Foreign Direct Investment
text:
FDI vs. portfolio investment

Direct investment: lasting interest and influence over management of a foreign enterprise (typically 10% or more of voting power).
Portfolio investment: cross-border holdings of securities without a direct-investment relationship.
Direct investment is closely linked to multinational production and global value chains; portfolio flows are generally more liquid and volatile.
